title: Law of Demand and Elasticity of Demand
outcomes: Define demand and explain its determinants and the demand function.
State the law of demand, derive market demand, explain why the curve slopes down, and list exceptions.
Distinguish expansion/contraction from increase/decrease in demand.
Measure price elasticity by the percentage, point, geometric, arc and total outlay methods, and explain its determinants.
Compute and interpret income, cross and advertisement elasticities.

meta.exam_tip: This is the heaviest-weighted unit of the chapter. Expect 4–6 MCQs: an elasticity calculation (percentage, arc or point), a total outlay classification, a shift-vs-movement question and a Giffen/Veblen exception. Always check which base the question wants.

concepts.title: Meaning of demand
body: In economics, demand is not mere desire. It is the desire for a good backed by the ability and the willingness to pay for it. A student who wants a car but cannot pay has a wish, not demand; a rich person who can pay but does not want it has no demand either.

Two points make the definition precise. First, quantity demanded is always stated at a particular price — at another price the quantity will be different. Second, demand is a flow: it is the quantity bought per unit of time (per day, week, month or year), not a one-off purchase. "Demand for milk is 5,000 litres" means nothing; "5,000 litres a day at ₹60 a litre" is a proper statement.
concepts.analogy: Demand is a wish with a wallet and a decision: all three must be present.
concepts.work: Sales budgets prepared by CAs are always stated as quantity per period at an assumed price — exactly the economist's definition of demand.

concepts.title: What determines demand
body: (1) Price of the good itself — usually more is bought at a lower price. (2) Prices of related goods — substitutes (tea and coffee; a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other) and complements (car and petrol, printer and cartridge; a rise in the price of one lowers demand for the other). (3) Disposable income of the consumer — for normal goods demand rises with income; for inferior goods (coarse grains, cheap substitutes) demand falls as income rises because buyers shift to better goods.

(4) Tastes and preferences — shaped by fashion, habit, advertising and social influence. Special effects: the demonstration effect (copying others' consumption), the bandwagon effect (buying because others are buying), the snob effect (buying less of a thing because many others have it), and the Veblen effect (wanting a costly good because its high price signals status). (5) Consumers' expectations — of future prices and incomes; if prices are expected to rise, people buy more now.

(6) Other factors — size of population; composition of population (age, gender, urban/rural mix); level of national income and its distribution (more equal distribution raises demand for wage goods, unequal distribution raises demand for luxuries); availability of consumer credit; and interest rates (cheap loans raise demand for durables like houses and cars).
concepts.analogy: Price is the steering wheel of demand; the other determinants are the road, weather and passengers — change any of them and the journey changes.
concepts.work: When a CA reviews a client's sales forecast, the assumptions to test are exactly these determinants: price plans, competitors' prices, income growth, consumer trends, credit availability and interest rates.

concepts.title: The demand function
body: A demand function states demand as a function of its determinants: Dx = f(Px, Py, M, T, A, U), where Px is the good's own price, Py prices of related goods, M money income, T tastes and preferences, A advertisement, and U other factors.

Since all determinants cannot be studied together, economists change one at a time and hold the rest constant (ceteris paribus). Holding everything except Px constant gives the price-demand relationship — the law of demand. A simple linear form is Q = a − bP: "a" captures the effect of all other determinants and "b" shows how much quantity falls when price rises by ₹1.
concepts.analogy: A demand function is a recipe: the dish (quantity demanded) depends on several ingredients, and to taste the effect of one spice you keep the others fixed.
concepts.work: Demand forecasting models built by analysts (often by regression) are estimated demand functions; their coefficients feed revenue projections in project reports.

concepts.title: The law of demand: schedule and curve
body: Law of demand: other things remaining the same, the quantity demanded of a good rises when its price falls and falls when its price rises — price and quantity demanded are inversely related.
Assumptions ("other things") include: no change in consumers' income, tastes and preferences, prices of related goods, expectations, and the size and composition of population.

An individual demand schedule is a table of prices and the quantities one buyer will purchase. A market demand schedule adds, at each price, the quantities demanded by all buyers in the market (horizontal summation). Plotting either gives a demand curve that slopes downward from left to right, with price on the Y-axis and quantity on the X-axis.
concepts.analogy: A demand curve is like a see-saw: when price goes up, quantity comes down.
concepts.work: Retail chains test the law of demand with "price-off" weeks; the extra units sold at the lower price are used to judge whether the discount paid for itself.

concepts.title: Why the demand curve slopes downward
body: (1) Law of diminishing marginal utility (Marshall): each additional unit gives less extra satisfaction, so a consumer buys more only if the price falls. (2) Price effect = substitution effect + income effect (Hicks and Allen): when price falls, the good becomes cheaper relative to substitutes, so buyers switch towards it (substitution effect); the fall also raises real income (purchasing power), so more can be bought (income effect). For a normal good both work in the same direction.

(3) Arrival of new consumers: a lower price brings in buyers who could not afford it before. (4) Different uses: at a lower price a good is put to more uses (electricity used for lighting, then also for heating and cooking).
concepts.analogy: When biryani gets cheaper, you eat more because the next plate is still worth the lower price (utility), you switch from pizza (substitution), you feel richer (income), and your friends who couldn't afford it join in (new buyers).
concepts.work: Pricing teams estimate how much of a sales jump after a price cut comes from new customers versus existing ones buying more — a practical use of these reasons.

concepts.title: Exceptions to the law of demand
body: (1) Conspicuous (prestige) goods — diamonds, luxury watches, designer bags: bought to display wealth, so a higher price can raise demand (Veblen effect). (2) Giffen goods — named after Sir Robert Giffen, who observed that when the price of bread rose, poor families bought more of it; a very inferior staple that takes a large share of a poor family's budget can show a rising demand curve because the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect. (3) Conspicuous necessities — goods like smartphones or televisions that have become social necessities and are bought even at higher prices. (4) Expectations of future prices — if prices are rising and expected to rise further, people buy more now even at the higher price.

(5) Incomplete information and irrational behaviour — buyers may judge quality by price or act on impulse. (6) Necessaries — demand for essentials like salt or basic medicines hardly changes with price. (7) Speculative goods — shares, gold or land: rising prices may trigger more buying in the hope of further rise.
Important: all Giffen goods are inferior goods, but not every inferior good is a Giffen good.
concepts.analogy: Exceptions are like people who leave a restaurant when prices fall — they think cheap means bad — or rush in when prices rise because they fear missing out.
concepts.work: Luxury brands avoid discounting for exactly this reason: a lower price can damage the "status" value and reduce demand. CAs advising such brands treat price as a positioning tool, not only a revenue tool.

concepts.title: Movement along vs shift of the demand curve
body: Expansion and contraction (change in quantity demanded) — caused only by a change in the good's own price, other things constant; shown as a movement along the same demand curve. A fall in price → expansion (move down the curve); a rise in price → contraction (move up the curve).

Increase and decrease (change in demand) — caused by a change in any other determinant (income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, population, credit). The whole curve shifts: rightward for an increase (more bought at the same price, or the same quantity at a higher price) and leftward for a decrease.

Examples: a rise in income shifts the demand curve for a normal good to the right but for an inferior good to the left; a rise in the price of tea shifts the coffee curve right; a rise in petrol prices shifts the demand curve for petrol cars left.

blocks.title: Four terms students mix up

concepts.analogy: Moving along the curve is walking along a road; a shift is the road itself being moved to a new place.
concepts.work: In variance analysis, a CA separates a sales change into a price effect (movement) and a market/volume effect from other causes (shift) — the same distinction.

concepts.title: Price elasticity of demand: meaning and degrees
body: Price elasticity of demand (Ep) measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a change in price: Ep = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price = (ΔQ/Q) × (P/ΔP). Because price and quantity move in opposite directions the result is negative; by convention the minus sign is dropped and the absolute value is read.

Degrees: perfectly inelastic (Ep = 0) — quantity does not change at all, vertical curve; relatively inelastic (0 < Ep < 1) — quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price; unitary elastic (Ep = 1) — equal percentages, curve is a rectangular hyperbola; relatively elastic (Ep > 1) — quantity changes by a larger percentage; perfectly elastic (Ep = ∞) — horizontal curve, the smallest price rise wipes out demand.

Elasticity is not the same as slope. Slope is ΔP/ΔQ in absolute units; elasticity uses percentages and depends on where you are on the curve. Comparing curves through the same point, the steeper one is less elastic there.
concepts.analogy: Elasticity is how far a rubber band stretches for the same pull. A thick band (salt) barely moves; a thin one (a particular brand of chips) stretches a lot.
concepts.work: Before recommending a price increase, a CA estimates elasticity: if demand is inelastic, revenue will rise; if elastic, it will fall.

concepts.title: Measuring price elasticity: percentage, point, geometric and arc methods
body: Percentage (proportionate) method: Ep = (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔP/P), with the original price and quantity as base.

Point elasticity: for a very small change at a point on the curve, Ep = −(dQ/dP) × (P/Q). For a linear demand Q = a − bP, dQ/dP = −b, so Ep = b × P/Q. It is the price-quantity ratio at the point multiplied by the reciprocal of the slope.

Geometric method on a straight-line demand curve: at any point R, Ep = lower segment ÷ upper segment (the part of the line below R to the quantity axis divided by the part above R to the price axis). So elasticity is infinite where the line meets the price axis, greater than 1 above the mid-point, exactly 1 at the mid-point, less than 1 below it, and zero where it meets the quantity axis — even though the slope is constant.

Arc elasticity (mid-point method) for large changes between two points: Ep = [(Q2 − Q1) ÷ (Q2 + Q1)] × [(P2 + P1) ÷ (P2 − P1)], absolute value. Using the averages as base gives the same answer whether price rises or falls; the arc value lies between the point elasticities at the two ends (not necessarily in the middle).

blocks.title: Choosing the method

concepts.analogy: Percentage method measures from where you started; the arc method measures from the middle of the bridge, so walking either way gives the same length.
concepts.work: Analysts use arc elasticity on before-and-after data from a price change, and point elasticity when they have an estimated demand equation.

concepts.title: Total outlay (total revenue) method
body: Total outlay (TO) by buyers = total revenue (TR) of sellers = P × Q. Watch how it changes when price changes:

If price falls and TO rises (or price rises and TO falls) — price and outlay move in opposite directions — demand is elastic (Ep > 1). If TO stays the same — demand is unitary elastic (Ep = 1). If price falls and TO falls (or price rises and TO rises) — same direction — demand is inelastic (Ep < 1).
Limitation: this method only tells whether demand is elastic, unitary or inelastic; it does not give the exact coefficient.
Business use: if demand is elastic, a price cut raises revenue; if inelastic, a price rise raises revenue. This is why the elasticity of demand matters so much for pricing.
concepts.analogy: Think of a shopkeeper's cash box: if a discount fills it more, customers are price-sensitive (elastic); if it empties it, they are not (inelastic).
concepts.work: Revenue impact analysis for a tariff change, a toll revision or a GST rate change uses exactly this logic.

concepts.title: Determinants of price elasticity of demand
body: (1) Availability of substitutes — the more and closer the substitutes, the more elastic (one brand of soap is elastic; salt in general is inelastic). (2) Position in the consumer's budget — goods taking a tiny share of income (matchboxes, salt) are inelastic; big-ticket items more elastic. (3) Number of uses — a good with many uses (electricity, milk) tends to be more elastic. (4) Nature of the good — necessities are inelastic, luxuries elastic. (5) Time period — demand is more elastic in the long run, as consumers find substitutes and change habits. (6) Habits and addiction — habitual goods (tea, cigarettes) are inelastic. (7) Possibility of postponing consumption — goods whose purchase can be postponed (durables) are more elastic. (8) Price range — very high-priced and very low-priced goods tend to be inelastic; elasticity is usually greater in the middle range. (9) Complementary goods — a good used jointly with another (ink with a pen) is usually inelastic. (10) Income level of buyers — the rich are less sensitive to price changes than the poor.
concepts.analogy: You are flexible about which café you visit (many substitutes) but not about buying medicine your doctor prescribed (no substitute, necessity).
concepts.work: Tax authorities prefer taxing goods with inelastic demand (fuel, tobacco) because revenue is stable; CAs advising on indirect-tax impact on sales use the same reasoning.

concepts.title: Income elasticity and cross elasticity of demand
body: Income elasticity (Ei) = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income = (ΔQ/Q) × (Y/ΔY). Ei > 1: income-elastic (luxuries) — demand grows faster than income. 0 < Ei < 1: income-inelastic (necessities such as food and medicines) — demand grows more slowly than income. Ei = 0: demand does not respond to income. Ei < 0: inferior goods — demand falls as income rises. All normal goods have positive Ei.
Link with budget share: if the share of income spent on a good stays the same as income rises, Ei = 1; if the share rises, Ei > 1; if the share falls, Ei < 1.

Cross elasticity (Ec) = % change in quantity demanded of X ÷ % change in price of Y. Positive for substitutes (tea price up → coffee demand up); negative for complements (car price up → petrol demand down); zero for unrelated goods. The larger the positive value, the closer the substitutes.
concepts.analogy: Income elasticity asks "what do you buy more of after a raise?"; cross elasticity asks "what happens to your coffee habit when tea gets dearer?"
concepts.work: Retailers planning store formats for rising-income towns stock more high-Ei goods; competition authorities use cross elasticity to define a "relevant market" in merger reviews.

concepts.title: Advertisement (promotional) elasticity
body: Advertisement elasticity of demand (Ea) measures how sales respond to a change in advertising spend: Ea = (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔA/A), where A is initial advertisement expenditure and ΔA the additional spend. It is usually positive and lies between zero and infinity.

Ea = 0: sales do not respond to more advertising. 0 < Ea < 1: sales rise less than proportionately. Ea = 1: sales rise in the same proportion. Ea > 1: sales rise more than proportionately. A higher value means a more effective campaign; firms use it to decide the optimum advertising budget.
concepts.analogy: Advertising is like watering a plant: up to a point growth responds well, after that extra water does little.
concepts.work: Marketing ROI reviews by finance teams compute exactly this ratio before approving the next campaign budget.

illustrations.title: Market demand schedule from individual schedules
illustrations.q: Three buyers, Asha, Bilal and Chetan, are the only buyers of a snack. Derive the market demand schedule and state the law of demand it shows.

solution.text: Market demand rises from 3 units at ₹50 to 30 units at ₹10 — price and quantity are inversely related, as the law of demand says. Note that Bilal enters the market only when the price falls below ₹50 — one reason the market curve slopes downward (new buyers).

illustrations.title: Price elasticity — percentage method and the revenue check
illustrations.q: When the price of a pen falls from ₹40 to ₹36, sales rise from 500 to 600 a week. Find the price elasticity of demand and confirm the result with the total outlay method.

solution.text: Ep = 2 > 1, so demand is elastic. Check: outlay rises from ₹20,000 to ₹21,600 when price falls — price and outlay move in opposite directions, confirming elastic demand.

illustrations.title: Arc elasticity — why the mid-point method is used
illustrations.q: At ₹80 a box, 200 boxes of dates are sold; at ₹60, 300 boxes. Find (a) arc elasticity, (b) elasticity with ₹80/200 as base, (c) elasticity with ₹60/300 as base. Comment.

solution.text: Comment: the simple percentage method gives 2 or 1 depending on the direction of change. The mid-point (arc) method gives one value, 1.4, either way, lying between the two.

checks.label: elasticity using old values as base
elasticity using new values as base (rising price from 60 to 80)

illustrations.title: Point elasticity from a demand equation
illustrations.q: The demand function is Q = 1,200 − 20P. Find the point elasticity at P = ₹40, ₹30 and ₹15, and identify the price at which demand is unitary elastic.

solution.text: dQ/dP = −20, so Ep = 20 × P ÷ Q (absolute value).

Demand meets the price axis at P = 60 (Q = 0). The mid-point of the line is at P = 30, Q = 600, where Ep = 1, exactly as the geometric rule (lower segment = upper segment) predicts. Above ₹30 demand is elastic; below it, inelastic — though the slope is the same everywhere.

illustrations.title: Total outlay method for three products
illustrations.q: Classify the price elasticity of demand for each product using the total outlay method.

solution.text: Price and outlay in the same direction → inelastic; opposite directions → elastic; unchanged outlay → unitary.

illustrations.title: Income, cross and advertisement elasticities
illustrations.q: A household's monthly income rises from ₹40,000 to ₹50,000. Its monthly purchases change: rice 20 kg → 22 kg; dining out 6 → 9 times; coarse grain 10 kg → 8 kg. Separately, when the price of tea rises from ₹200 to ₹240 a kg, a café's coffee sales rise from 50 to 60 kg; when the price of a cartridge rises from ₹100 to ₹120, printer sales fall from 1,000 to 900. A firm raises advertising from ₹2,00,000 to ₹3,00,000 and sales rise from 10,000 to 12,500 units. Compute and interpret each elasticity.

checks.label: cross elasticity coffee w.r.t. tea price
cross elasticity of printer demand w.r.t. cartridge price

jobs.title: Should the gym raise its membership fee?
jobs.role: CA advising a fitness chain (small business client)
jobs.situation: The client wants to raise the monthly fee from ₹2,000 to ₹2,200. Last year, a 5% rise led to a 9% drop in members.
steps: Estimate elasticity from past data: 9% ÷ 5% = 1.8 — elastic.
Predict the effect of a 10% rise: members may fall about 18%, so revenue falls (elastic demand).
Check determinants: many nearby gyms (substitutes) explain the high elasticity.
Advise differentiation (classes, timing, trainers) to lower elasticity before raising prices, or offer an annual plan instead.
jobs.takeaway: With elastic demand, price rises cut revenue; reduce elasticity first by differentiating the product.
jobs.think: Approximately what will happen to revenue if the fee rises 10% and members fall 18%?
jobs.answer: Revenue becomes about 1.10 × 0.82 = 0.902 of the old level — roughly a 10% fall.

jobs.title: Forecasting demand for a premium product line
jobs.role: CA in industry — FP&A analyst at a consumer goods company
jobs.situation: Management expects household incomes in its markets to rise 8% next year and asks for a sales forecast for premium chocolates (income elasticity about 1.5) and basic biscuits (about 0.4).
steps: Apply income elasticity: premium chocolates +1.5 × 8% = +12%; basic biscuits +0.4 × 8% = +3.2%.
Adjust for planned price changes using price elasticity.
Shift marketing and capacity planning towards the high-Ei product.
jobs.takeaway: Income elasticity converts macro forecasts (income growth) into product-level sales forecasts.

jobs.title: Was the advertising campaign worth it?
jobs.role: Articled assistant in a management audit
jobs.situation: A client doubled ad spend from ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh; sales rose from 50,000 to 60,000 units at a contribution of ₹80 per unit.
steps: Extra contribution = 10,000 × ₹80 = ₹8,00,000, less than the extra ₹10,00,000 spent.
Report that the campaign did not pay for itself at the margin.
jobs.takeaway: Low advertisement elasticity can make additional advertising unprofitable.

mcqs.q: Demand in economics means:
options: Desire backed by ability and willingness to pay
mcqs.explain: In economics, demand means desire backed by both the ability to pay and the willingness to pay, at a given price and time. "Desire for a good" is the trap — wanting a car without the money, or having the money but no intention to spend it, creates no demand. In practice: a carmaker estimating demand counts households that can afford the EMI and are ready to buy, not everyone who likes the car.

mcqs.q: Demand is a flow concept because it is expressed:
mcqs.explain: Demand is a flow: it is a quantity per unit of time — litres of milk per day or phones per month. "At one point of time" is the trap; that describes a stock, such as the inventory sitting in a warehouse today. In practice: a dairy like Amul plans procurement on daily demand, because "1 lakh litres" means nothing until you say per day or per week.

mcqs.q: Tea and coffee are:
mcqs.explain: Tea and coffee satisfy the same want, so they are substitutes: if coffee becomes dearer, some buyers switch to tea and demand for tea rises. "Complements" is the trap — complements are used together, like tea and sugar, so a price rise of one reduces demand for the other. In practice: café chains in India watch tea prices because a sharp rise in coffee prices sends customers to chai.

mcqs.q: A fall in the price of cars is likely to:
mcqs.explain: Cars and petrol are complements, used together. A fall in car prices raises the number of cars bought, which in turn increases the demand for petrol — a rightward shift in petrol demand. "Decrease the demand for petrol" is the trap; that would be true only for substitutes. In practice: oil marketing companies factor in vehicle sales data when forecasting fuel demand.

mcqs.q: For an inferior good, a rise in consumer income:
mcqs.explain: An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises, because buyers move to better alternatives — for example, from coarse grains to fine rice. "Increases demand" is the trap; that is the behaviour of a normal good. In practice: FMCG companies notice that as rural incomes rise, sales of loose, unbranded products fall while branded packaged products gain.

mcqs.q: Buying less of a product because many others have started using it is called the:
mcqs.explain: The snob effect is buying less of a product as more people start using it, because snobs value exclusivity. "Bandwagon effect" is the trap — it is the exact opposite: buying more because others are buying. In practice: luxury brands deliberately keep supply limited and prices high so that their handbags and watches do not become common and lose snob appeal.

mcqs.q: The tendency to buy a good because others are buying it is the:
mcqs.explain: The bandwagon effect is the tendency to buy a good because others are buying it — people want to join the crowd and stay in fashion. "Snob effect" is the trap; snobs do the reverse and drop a product once it becomes popular. In practice: smartphone launches and viral food trends in Indian cities see demand snowball as friends and influencers adopt them.

mcqs.q: In the demand function Dx = f(Px, Py, M, T, A, U), "M" stands for:
mcqs.explain: In the demand function Dx = f(Px, Py, M, T, A, U), M stands for the consumer's money income; Px is own price, Py prices of related goods, T tastes, A advertising and U other factors. "Market size" is the trap — it does affect market demand, but M in this function denotes income. In practice: forecasting models for consumer durables use household income as a key explanatory variable.

mcqs.q: Holding all other determinants constant, the law of demand tells us that:
options: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related
Price and quantity demanded are directly related
mcqs.explain: The law of demand states that, other things remaining constant, price and quantity demanded are inversely related: a lower price brings a larger quantity demanded, a higher price a smaller one. "Directly related" is the trap — that describes the law of supply. In practice: e-commerce sale days in India see order volumes surge exactly because prices are cut while incomes and tastes remain unchanged.

mcqs.q: The market demand curve is obtained by:
options: Horizontal summation of individual demand curves
Vertical summation of individual demand curves
mcqs.explain: The market demand curve is found by horizontal summation: at each price, the quantities demanded by all buyers are added up. "Vertical summation" is the trap — that would add prices at a given quantity, which is used for public goods, not ordinary market demand. In practice: a cinema estimates total ticket demand at ₹200 by adding what each customer segment would buy at that price.

mcqs.q: According to Hicks and Allen, the demand curve slopes downward because of:
mcqs.explain: Hicks and Allen explained the downward slope through the price effect, which splits into the substitution effect (the good becomes relatively cheaper) and the income effect (real income rises). "Diminishing marginal utility only" is the trap; that was Marshall's explanation using cardinal utility. In practice: when petrol prices fall, people both drive more instead of using alternatives and feel slightly richer.

mcqs.q: Marshall explained the downward slope of the demand curve with the:
mcqs.explain: Marshall used the law of diminishing marginal utility: since each extra unit gives less satisfaction, a consumer buys more only if price falls. "Indifference curve" is the trap — that is the ordinal tool used later by Hicks and Allen. In practice: "buy two, get the third at half price" offers work because the third unit is worth less to the buyer, so it needs a lower price.

mcqs.q: A Giffen good is:
options: An inferior good whose demand rises when its price rises
A good with perfectly elastic demand
mcqs.explain: A Giffen good is an inferior good on which poor households spend a large share of income; when its price rises, the strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so quantity demanded rises. "A luxury good" is the trap — luxuries have high positive income elasticity, the opposite of inferior goods. In practice: Giffen behaviour has been reported for staples among very poor households, such as rice in China.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct?
options: All Giffen goods are inferior, but not all inferior goods are Giffen goods
All inferior goods are Giffen goods
Giffen goods have positive income elasticity
mcqs.explain: Every Giffen good is inferior, because the paradox needs a negative income effect; but most inferior goods are not Giffen goods, since their substitution effect still outweighs the income effect. "All inferior goods are Giffen goods" is the trap — it reverses the relationship. In practice: cheap coarse grains are inferior for many Indian households, yet their demand still falls when their price rises.

mcqs.q: Demand for diamonds rising when their price rises illustrates:
mcqs.explain: Diamonds are conspicuous or Veblen goods: their prestige comes partly from a high price, so a price rise can increase demand among status-seekers. "Giffen paradox" is the trap — it also shows a rising price raising demand, but it applies to cheap inferior staples bought by the poor, not luxuries. In practice: jewellers rarely advertise discounts on premium diamonds, because a low price would dent their status appeal.

mcqs.q: A fall in the price of a good, other things constant, causes:
options: Expansion of demand — movement down the same curve
mcqs.explain: A change in the good's own price, with other factors constant, causes a movement along the same demand curve; a price fall leads to expansion of demand — a move downward along the curve. "Increase in demand — rightward shift" is the trap; shifts are caused by non-price factors like income or tastes. In practice: when an airline cuts fares, more tickets are bought along its existing demand curve.

mcqs.q: A rise in consumers' income shifts the demand curve for a normal good to the:
options: Neither — it is a movement along the curve
mcqs.explain: Income is a non-price determinant, so a change in income shifts the whole demand curve. For a normal good, higher income means more is demanded at every price — a shift to the right. "Neither — it is a movement along the curve" is the trap; movements occur only when the good's own price changes. In practice: salary increases after a Pay Commission push up demand for cars and housing at existing prices.

mcqs.q: Which of the following causes a leftward shift of the demand curve for coffee?
options: A fall in the price of tea
A rise in the price of tea
A fall in the price of coffee
A rise in income (coffee being normal)
mcqs.explain: Tea is a substitute for coffee; if tea becomes cheaper, some coffee drinkers switch, so less coffee is demanded at every price — a leftward shift. "A fall in the price of coffee" is the trap; a change in coffee's own price causes a movement along the curve, not a shift. In practice: a coffee chain tracks rival tea-shop pricing because a cheaper substitute can shift its demand curve.

mcqs.q: When demand is perfectly inelastic, the demand curve is:
mcqs.explain: Perfectly inelastic demand (elasticity = 0) means quantity does not change at all whatever the price, so the demand curve is a vertical line. "Horizontal" is the trap — a horizontal curve shows perfectly elastic demand, where elasticity is infinite. In practice: a patient's demand for a life-saving drug like insulin is close to perfectly inelastic, which is why such drug prices are regulated by the NPPA.

mcqs.q: A demand curve with unitary elasticity throughout is a:
mcqs.explain: With unitary elasticity everywhere, total expenditure (P × Q) stays the same at every price; a curve on which P × Q is constant is a rectangular hyperbola. "Straight line" is the trap — elasticity changes along a straight-line demand curve, from infinite at the price axis to zero at the quantity axis. In practice: a household that keeps a fixed monthly budget for fruit, whatever the price, behaves as if demand were unit elastic.

mcqs.q: Price of a pen falls from ₹40 to ₹36 and sales rise from 500 to 600. Price elasticity (percentage method) is:
mcqs.explain: Percentage method: %ΔQ = (600 − 500)/500 = 20%; %ΔP = (40 − 36)/40 = 10%; elasticity = 20 ÷ 10 = 2. 0.5 is the trap — it divides the price change by the quantity change, inverting the formula. In practice: a stationery brand learns that a 10% price cut boosts pen sales by 20%, so the cut raises revenue — useful before a back-to-school promotion.

mcqs.q: Price falls from ₹80 to ₹60 and quantity rises from 200 to 300. Arc elasticity is:
mcqs.explain: Arc elasticity uses averages: (ΔQ ÷ (Q1 + Q2)) × ((P1 + P2) ÷ ΔP) = (100/500) × (140/20) = 0.2 × 7 = 1.4. 2 is the trap — it uses the original values (200 and 80) as the base; using the new values gives 1. The arc method avoids this base problem. In practice: analysts use arc elasticity when prices change a lot, such as after a big GST rate cut.

mcqs.q: For the demand function Q = 1,200 − 20P, point elasticity at P = ₹40 is:
mcqs.explain: At P = 40, Q = 1,200 − 20 × 40 = 400. Point elasticity = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q) = 20 × 40/400 = 2 (ignoring the minus sign). 20 is the trap — it is only the slope coefficient, which must be multiplied by P/Q. 0.5 inverts the result. In practice: pricing teams estimate a demand equation from sales data and read elasticity at the current price before changing it.

mcqs.q: On a straight-line demand curve, at the mid-point elasticity is:
mcqs.explain: On a straight-line demand curve, point elasticity = lower segment ÷ upper segment. At the mid-point the two segments are equal, so elasticity = 1. "Greater than 1" is the trap — that holds above the mid-point, nearer the price axis. In practice: this is why a firm facing a linear demand curve earns maximum revenue at the mid-point, where marginal revenue is zero.

mcqs.q: On a straight-line demand curve, the point where it meets the quantity axis has elasticity:
mcqs.explain: Point elasticity = lower segment ÷ upper segment. Where the curve meets the quantity axis, the lower segment is zero, so elasticity = 0. "Infinity" is the trap — that occurs at the other end, where the line meets the price axis and the upper segment is zero. In practice: at very low prices, buyers are already saturated, so further price cuts add little to sales, as with heavily discounted salt.

mcqs.q: A fall in price leads to a fall in total expenditure on a good. Demand is:
mcqs.explain: Under the total outlay method, if price and total expenditure move in the same direction, demand is inelastic: the fall in price is not offset by enough extra quantity. "Elastic" is the trap — with elastic demand, a price cut raises total outlay. In practice: farmers often earn less in a bumper-crop year, because prices fall sharply while demand for staples is inelastic.

mcqs.q: Price of a toy rises from ₹100 to ₹120 and quantity falls from 300 to 250. Total outlay method shows demand is:
mcqs.explain: Total outlay before = 100 × 300 = ₹30,000; after = 120 × 250 = ₹30,000. Outlay is unchanged although price changed, so demand is unitary elastic by the total outlay method. "Elastic" is the trap — quantity did fall, but not by enough to reduce total spending. In practice: a toy retailer checks the till total, not just units sold, to judge whether a price change paid off.

mcqs.q: The main limitation of the total outlay method is that it:
options: Cannot give the exact numerical value of elasticity
mcqs.explain: The total outlay method only classifies demand as elastic, unitary or inelastic from the direction of change in spending; it cannot give an exact numerical value. "Needs a demand equation" is the trap — that is required for the point method, not the outlay method, which needs only prices and spending. In practice: a shop owner can tell from sales records that demand is elastic, but needs the percentage method to say by how much.

mcqs.q: Demand for a good with many close substitutes is likely to be:
mcqs.explain: When many close substitutes exist, even a small price rise drives buyers to rival products, so demand is elastic. "Inelastic" is the trap — it applies to goods with few or no substitutes, such as salt or medicines. In practice: a single brand of bottled water faces elastic demand because shoppers can easily pick another brand at the same shop.

mcqs.q: Price elasticity of demand is generally greater in the:
mcqs.explain: Elasticity is greater in the long run, because consumers have time to find substitutes, change habits and adjust equipment. "Short run" is the trap — in the short run people are locked into habits and existing appliances, so they respond less. In practice: after petrol prices rose, many Indian buyers switched to CNG or electric vehicles over the following years, not overnight.

mcqs.q: Income rises from ₹40,000 to ₹50,000 and demand for rice rises from 20 kg to 22 kg. Income elasticity is:
mcqs.explain: Income elasticity = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔY = ((22 − 20)/20) ÷ ((50,000 − 40,000)/40,000) = 10% ÷ 25% = 0.4. A value between 0 and 1 marks rice as a necessity. 2.5 is the trap — it divides income change by quantity change, inverting the formula. In practice: FMCG and food companies expect staple sales to grow more slowly than incomes and plan capacity accordingly.

mcqs.q: Income elasticity of demand for an inferior good is:
mcqs.explain: For an inferior good, demand falls as income rises, so the change in quantity and the change in income have opposite signs — income elasticity is negative. "Between 0 and 1" is the trap; that range belongs to necessities, which are normal goods. In practice: rising household incomes in India have reduced demand for kerosene as a cooking fuel in favour of LPG, a pattern of inferior-good behaviour.

mcqs.q: If the proportion of income spent on a good rises as income rises, its income elasticity is:
mcqs.explain: If the share of income spent on a good rises as income rises, its demand is growing faster than income, so income elasticity is greater than one — a luxury. "Equal to one" is the trap; then the share would stay exactly constant. In practice: as Indian incomes rise, spending on foreign holidays and dining out grows faster than income, so travel firms target the rising middle class.

mcqs.q: Cross elasticity of demand between two complementary goods is:
mcqs.explain: For complements, a rise in the price of one reduces the demand for the other, so the two changes have opposite signs and cross elasticity is negative. "Positive" is the trap — positive cross elasticity identifies substitutes. In practice: printer makers price printers low and cartridges high, knowing the two are complements, so a cheaper printer lifts cartridge sales.

mcqs.q: Cartridge price rises from ₹100 to ₹120 and printer sales fall from 1,000 to 900. Cross elasticity is:
mcqs.explain: Cross elasticity = %Δ printer sales ÷ %Δ cartridge price = ((900 − 1,000)/1,000) ÷ ((120 − 100)/100) = −10% ÷ 20% = −0.5. The negative sign confirms complements. +0.5 is the trap — dropping the sign hides the relationship, which is the whole point of cross elasticity. In practice: competition regulators such as the CCI use cross elasticity to judge which products belong to the same market.

mcqs.q: Advertising spend rises from ₹2,00,000 to ₹3,00,000 and sales from 10,000 to 12,500 units. Advertisement elasticity is:
mcqs.explain: Advertisement elasticity = %Δ sales ÷ %Δ advertising = ((12,500 − 10,000)/10,000) ÷ ((3,00,000 − 2,00,000)/2,00,000) = 25% ÷ 50% = 0.5. 2 is the trap — it divides the advertising change by the sales change, inverting the formula. In practice: a marketing head uses this ratio to judge whether an extra ₹1 lakh of advertising adds enough sales to justify itself.

mcqs.q: An advertisement elasticity greater than one means:
options: Sales rise more than proportionately to advertising spend
mcqs.explain: Advertisement elasticity above one means a given percentage rise in advertising spend raises sales by a larger percentage — advertising is highly effective. "Sales rise less than proportionately" is the trap; that describes an elasticity between 0 and 1. In practice: newly launched brands often show high advertising elasticity, which is why start-ups spend heavily on digital ads during launch.

questions.q: A firm cuts the price of its water purifier filter from ₹100 to ₹90; monthly sales rise from 1,500 to 1,800 units. (a) Compute price elasticity of demand by the percentage method. (b) Verify using the total outlay method. (c) Should the firm cut the price further, assuming costs allow it? Show steps.

model.text: (a) Ep = 2 (elastic). (b) Outlay rises from ₹1,50,000 to ₹1,62,000 as price falls — opposite directions, elastic. (c) With elastic demand, a further cut raises revenue; whether profit rises depends on the cost of the extra units, so the firm should compare the extra revenue with the extra cost.

(d) Is the change in (c) a movement along the demand curve or a shift?

model.text: (a) Ep = 1.5: elastic. (b) Demand is unitary elastic at P = ₹25 (Q = 1,000). (c) Ei = 1: normal good; the share of income spent on it stays the same (borderline between necessity and luxury). (d) Income changed while price stayed the same — the whole demand curve shifts to the right (increase in demand), not a movement along it.

Exceptions: Veblen/conspicuous goods, Giffen goods, conspicuous necessities, price expectations, irrational behaviour, necessaries, speculative goods.

cases.title: BrewFresh coffee capsules — pricing, promotion and incomes
cases.case: BrewFresh sells coffee capsules in a city. Last quarter it cut the price of a box from ₹250 to ₹200 and monthly sales rose from 4,000 to 5,600 boxes. In another month, with price unchanged, it raised its advertising budget from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,50,000 and sales rose from 4,000 to 4,600 boxes. A survey shows that when average household income in the city rose from ₹30,000 to ₹33,000 a month, sales rose from 4,000 to 4,400 boxes at an unchanged price. A rival tea-capsule brand is planning a price cut.

mcqs.q: Price elasticity of demand for BrewFresh capsules (percentage method, original values as base) is:
mcqs.explain: Using original values as base: %ΔQ = (5,600 − 4,000)/4,000 = 40%; %ΔP = (250 − 200)/250 = 20%; elasticity = 40 ÷ 20 = 2. 1.6 is the trap — it takes ₹200 as the base, giving a 25% price change; 0.5 inverts the ratio. In practice: knowing demand is this elastic tells BrewFresh that discounts can raise revenue, as long as margins cover costs.

mcqs.q: What happened to BrewFresh's total revenue after the price cut?
options: Rose from ₹10,00,000 to ₹11,20,000, confirming elastic demand
Fell from ₹10,00,000 to ₹11,20,000, showing inelastic demand
mcqs.explain: Revenue before = 250 × 4,000 = ₹10,00,000; after = 200 × 5,600 = ₹11,20,000. Price fell and total revenue rose, so demand is elastic, consistent with an elasticity of 2. The option saying revenue "fell" to ₹11,20,000 is the trap — the figures show a rise. In practice: finance teams compare revenue before and after a price promotion to confirm elasticity before repeating it.

mcqs.q: Advertisement elasticity of demand is:
mcqs.explain: Advertisement elasticity = %Δ sales ÷ %Δ advertising = ((4,600 − 4,000)/4,000) ÷ ((1,50,000 − 1,00,000)/1,00,000) = 15% ÷ 50% = 0.3. 0.15 is the trap — it is only the percentage change in sales, not yet divided by the change in advertising; 3.33 inverts the ratio. In practice: an elasticity of 0.3 tells BrewFresh that a price cut has been a stronger sales lever than extra advertising.

mcqs.q: Income elasticity of demand for the capsules is:
mcqs.explain: Income elasticity = ((4,400 − 4,000)/4,000) ÷ ((33,000 − 30,000)/30,000) = 10% ÷ 10% = 1. Demand rises in exact proportion to income, so the share of income spent on capsules stays constant. 0.1 is the trap — it is only the percentage change in quantity. In practice: market researchers use such figures to project how sales will grow as a city's incomes rise.

mcqs.q: If the rival cuts the price of tea capsules, BrewFresh's demand curve will most likely:
options: Show a movement down the same curve
mcqs.explain: Tea capsules are substitutes for coffee capsules. If the rival cuts its price, some buyers switch, so BrewFresh sells less at every price — its demand curve shifts to the left. "A movement down the same curve" is the trap; movements happen only when BrewFresh's own price changes. In practice: brands track competitors' price cuts closely, because a rival's discount can shrink their demand overnight.
